issues.item: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, a trigger based on being in a similar natural environment is hard to reconcile unless the robbery specifically occurred in wilderness or outdoors; nothing else in the profile supports that context, making this trigger clinically incongruent with the rest of the presentation.

Helicopter/aircraft sounds are not a plausible trauma-linked trigger for a mugging/robbery in the absence of any supporting memory or threat content suggesting emergency-response, combat, or disaster context. This appears disconnected from the trauma type and the rest of the selected items.

For a mugging/robbery trauma, helicopter/aircraft sounds are hard to link clinically unless the robbery specifically involved aircraft or a major police response; this trigger is not supported by the other selected items and feels trauma-incongruent.

Alcohol smell could occur if the perpetrator had been drinking, but that link is not reflected anywhere else in the profile, so as selected it appears weakly grounded in the trauma narrative compared with the other more plausible interpersonal-danger cues.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma in a 67-year-old male, contamination and body-focused shame are hard to reconcile unless there was a sexual assault or severe bodily violation component, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile. These appraisals fit poorly with the stated trauma type and with the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Burnt smell is a highly specific trigger that suggests fire, smoke, or explosion exposure. In a robbery/mugging profile it lacks support from the threat and appraisal items and does not connect plausibly to the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery in a 67-year-old male, 'body shame' is hard to reconcile unless there was prominent sexual assault, disfigurement, or injury-focused trauma content, which is not reflected elsewhere in threat, memory, or strategies. It reads as a qualitatively different appraisal from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: 'Burnt smell' is not a plausible trigger for a mugging/robbery unless there was specific fire/smoke/burning content in the trauma, which is not supported by the other selected items. It appears disconnected from the stated trauma type and from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery victim, 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the least coherent item in the profile. The rest of the report centers on external danger and mistrust (suspicious people, loud noises, hypervigilance, alarm when touched, mistrust, humiliation), but this item implies morally dissonant behaviour by the patient during the event. That is possible, but without any supporting memory or strategy content it stands apart from the otherwise victimization-focused formulation and is harder to reconcile clinically than the other items. The remaining items are broadly coherent with robbery trauma and with the active formulation path Negative Appraisals → Threat and Threat → Triggers.

vignette:
Gerald Whitmore is a 67-year-old hotel manager, married for over thirty years, who presents with a PCL-5 score of 62 following a mugging that occurred approximately eight months ago in the parking structure adjacent to the downtown hotel he manages. Gerald had worked late that evening, something he had done without incident for decades, and was walking to his car when a man approached him from behind a concrete pillar. The assailant smelled strongly of alcohol - Gerald would later describe it as the first thing that registered before the violence - and demanded his wallet and keys. When Gerald hesitated, the man grabbed him by the collar, shoved him hard against a parked car, and struck him across the face before fleeing with his belongings. The entire episode lasted perhaps ninety seconds. Gerald lay on the cold concrete for several minutes before a security camera operator noticed him on a monitor and sent help. He was 67 years old, alone in a structure he had considered safe, and he had been unable to do anything.

In the weeks that followed, Gerald found himself reorganizing his understanding of the world around what had happened to him. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt entirely rational to him, that people simply cannot be trusted - that the veneer of civility is thin and that anyone could be concealing dangerous intentions. More than this, he felt permanently humiliated, not only by the assault itself but by what he experienced as his own helplessness, his inability to protect himself, the image of a grown man crumpled against a car door in his own workplace. These appraisals - that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that he had been exposed as vulnerable - took root quickly and began to organize his behavior. Because he was now certain that threat was everywhere and that his own judgment about safety had once failed him catastrophically, he moved through daily life in a state of sustained alertness, scanning for danger with an exhausting thoroughness. He felt on guard even inside his own home, checking the locks multiple times each evening, sitting with his back to walls, unable to fully settle. His wife, Diane, noticed that he flinched badly if she touched his shoulder from behind - a habit she had never thought twice about in thirty years of marriage - and she eventually stopped initiating physical contact, uncertain of what he needed.

Because Gerald remained convinced that the world was dangerous and that his vigilance was the only thing standing between him and another assault, his heightened state of threat monitoring made him acutely sensitive to anything that resembled the conditions of that night. At work, which had once been his domain of competence and authority, the lobby and corridors of the hotel had become a landscape of potential threat. A guest moving in a way that seemed purposeful or unpredictable, someone lingering near an entrance, a patron whose behavior he could not immediately read - all of it now registered as suspicious and required his full attention. The smell of alcohol, which in a hotel bar is entirely ordinary, had become one of the most potent cues he encountered; when it reached him, something in him went cold and alert, as though the parking structure were reassembling itself around him. Loud noises - a luggage cart dropped, a door slamming, a burst of laughter from the bar - produced a startle response he could not suppress, and he had begun to find reasons to avoid the ground floor during peak evening hours, delegating tasks he had previously handled himself. His deputy manager had noticed and asked, with genuine concern, whether Gerald was all right. Gerald told him he was fine.

What finally brought Gerald to seek help was a conversation with Diane, who told him quietly one evening that she felt she was living with a stranger. He had not realized, until she said it, how completely he had withdrawn. He came to the first session hoping, in his words, to "get back to normal" - though he was privately unsure whether normal still existed for him, or whether the man who had walked through that parking structure without fear was simply gone.
